To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) DQB1*0102, *0201 and *0302 are protective alleles; (ii) DQB1 alleles *0202 and *0503 are susceptible; (iii) DRB1*1101 and *1301 are protective alleles; and (iv) DRB1 alleles *0402, *0404 and *1302 are susceptible.

the binding groove of DR4 and DR5 alleles can accommodate the Dsg3 960–977 peptide, and that DRB1 *0402 and DQA1 *0301 alleles play a crucial role in PV development by binding the Dsg3 peptide 960–977 with high affinity.
the structural aspects of the binding of Dsg3 peptides to MHC class II molecules are allele-specific, and that the binding specificity of DRB1*04 alleles may differ from that of DQB1*05 alleles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular basis of DR4 and DR5 susceptibility to PV and DR6 resistance to PV.
a comprehensive structural analysis of the DR and DQ binding groove, and provides a rational basis for understanding the molecular basis of PV susceptibility and resistance.
understanding the structural basis of the interaction between PV-associated peptides and MHC class II alleles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DR4 and DRB1*0301 alleles have a high binding affinity to the PV-associated peptides.
DRB1 and DQB alleles are not interchangeable in PV, but rather that each allele is associated with its own specific repertoire of Dsg3 peptides.
Dsg3 peptides have a high propensity for binding to the PV-associated alleles DRB1*0301 and DQB1 *0201, and a low propensity for binding to protective alleles DRB1 *0401 and DQB 1 *0201.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DRB1*04:01 and *07:01 alleles are the primary risk alleles for DR4 and DR7 PV, respectively.
the binding groove of the DR and DQ alleles is not a simple linear binding site, but rather a complex binding pocket, with multiple binding sites for Dsg3 peptides.
DRB1 alleles have a more significant role than the DQB1 alleles in the selection of self peptides in PV.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the structural analysis of the bound conformation is a useful tool to predict peptide binding to MHC Class I and II alleles and may be useful to identify new epitopes for the development of vaccines against autoimmune disorders.
the binding groove of the MHC Class II alleles is not a passive binding site, but a dynamic structure that can accommodate a variety of peptides.
PV-associated peptides are not random, but are rather selected by the disease associated DR and DQ alleles, and that these alleles may have different specificities for the same Dsg3 peptide.
